extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history/literary criticism (interested in symbolism, personification, and iconography)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or composing personifications and symbolic systems in literature and visual art (especially medieval/Renaissance religious art), with attention to spiritual depth, iconographic accuracy, and expressive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing duties with virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes a weakness in certain lists: 'the confusion of duties with virtues, and the vain endeavor to enumerate the various offices of charity as so many separate virtues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat discrete charitable acts or offices as distinct moral virtues. Maintain the conceptual distinction between moral virtues (dispositions of character) and particular duties/works. Avoid inflating classification by listing duties as virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid morbid accuracy of classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin critiques a tendency to 'morbid accuracy of classification' associated with Renaissance tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist over-systematising or pedantically subdividing virtues/ideas; excessive classification can weaken spiritual or artistic effect. Let classification serve meaning, not replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer symbolism over mere personification for spiritual depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: 'Personification is, in some sort, the reverse of symbolism, and is far less noble. Symbolism is the setting forth of a great truth by an imperfect and inferior sign ... Men who use symbolism forcibly are almost always true believers in what they symbolize.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symbolism (signs that point beyond themselves) when aiming for serious, spiritual, or mysterious expression. Personification (giving an abstract a human form) is more apt for fanciful or recreational treatment and can undermine belief in the thing personified unless handled with deep conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure personification is spiritualized and earnest
rubrics_metrics.description: Though personification is often inferior, 'in the hands of its early and earnest masters ... personification is often thoroughly noble and lovely.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using personification, infuse it with spiritual seriousness and intellectual power (as in Dante or early masters) so it complements rather than trivializes the idea. Avoid superficial or purely decorative personifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the system of virtues to the context/audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin observes that 'the number and nature of the virtues differ considerably in the statements of different poets and painters, according to their own views of religion, or to the manner of life they had it in mind to illustrate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose which virtues to personify according to the intended religious, social, or institutional context (e.g., monkish virtues at Assisi vs civic virtues for a palace). Align the selection with the work's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opposing vices/contraries to clarify a virtue's meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: when Prudence is opposed by Folly, it indicates Prudence means Heavenly Wisdom; 'reasoning from contraries is a great help' (especially in Dante).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pairings of virtue and vice deliberately to reveal the exact moral sense intended. Contrasts can sharpen interpretation and provide viewers/readers with clearer moral taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification should not disturb belief in the thing personified
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin warns that personification 'is apt to disturb the belief in the reality of the thing personified.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treatments that render an abstract idea ridiculous or merely theatrical; maintain dignity so the audience still accepts the underlying ideal as real or weighty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early/primitive forms often have greater spiritual vitality than later refinements
rubrics_metrics.description: The text claims 'the earlier conditions of it being just as much more spiritual and vital than the later ones, as the still earlier symbolism was more spiritual than they.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for spiritual expressiveness, study earlier, less 'polished' examples—they often convey more power and sincerity than later, more mannered versions. Polishing should not erase essential vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic attributes must convey character explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin repeatedly cites attributes (cross and key for Faith; coins poured from the lap for Liberality; a dagger and hair-tearing for Despair) as essential to reading figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give personified figures clear, intelligible attributes and inscriptions so viewers/readers can identify them; attributes should reinforce the moral or psychological content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscriptions aid intelligibility and should be used carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Several capitals bear inscriptions that identify virtues (e.g., 'lakgitas me onorat', 'discordia sum, DISCORDANS'); elsewhere the lack of inscription makes subjects unintelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use textual labels where iconography might be ambiguous; but ensure inscriptions are legible and correctly rendered to preserve meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain expressive detail and lifelikeness in figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between 'children of the fourteenth century ... full of youthful life ... keenness' and 'children of the fifteenth century ... dull smooth-faced dunces.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptural/poetic figures should preserve vitality and expressive detail (sharp features, lively expression) rather than bland idealisation; such detail communicates character and moral tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reductive or vulgar conceptualizations of virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance is often confused with mere abstinence in the Venetian conceit; Ruskin contrasts this with the Greek Temperance as 'the moderator of all the passions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent virtues in their full philosophical/theological scope rather than reducing them to narrow or commonplace senses (e.g., temperance = self-moderation, not just refraining from gluttony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic systems should be internally coherent and purposeful
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons: Dante's elaborate, classified Inferno and Purgatorio; Spenser's more complicated, unfinished system; different series (Giotto, Orcagna, Memmi) vary by aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design an underlying system (which virtues, which vices, their order and relationships) that coheres with the work's moral/architectural program; complexity is permissible but must serve comprehension and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/contextual appropriateness of virtues (regional differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin notes Northern art/morality stresses Industry and Honesty; Venetian lists include virtues like Modesty and Alacrity, while Assisi emphasises Chastity, Obedience, Poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select virtues and modes of depiction that reflect the cultural and moral priorities of the place/audience represented; iconography should resonate with local ethical ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid physical imagery to express moral/spiritual states
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser's Captain of the Lusts: wasting body, tiger, flint-headed arrows—'the horror and the truth of this are beyond everything...' used to show inner depravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concrete, often gruesome or striking physical details to make spiritual corruption or virtue emotionally and sensorially convincing; metaphor in bodily terms can deepen impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate pairing of virtues with their opposing vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples throughout: Liberality opposes Avarice; Despair opposes Hope; Patience's opponent is Impatience/Passion; Temperance opposed by Anger in Giotto's scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing a moral sequence, explicitly pair virtues with corresponding vices to clarify moral teaching and to allow didactic contrasts in imagery and narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic detail should reflect philosophical nuance (not mere labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Prudence is opposed by Folly, the folly is depicted eating fruit and brandishing a club to indicate sensuality and violence leading to atheism; such detail reveals nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond labels: choose gestures, objects, posture, and related motifs that express the deeper philosophical meaning of the virtue or vice, enabling richer interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect original compositional intent; avoid injurious 'Renaissance' alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin comments that in copies 'the changes thus made in the Renaissance pillars are always injuries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When restoring, copying, or adapting older works, preserve essential compositional and iconographic features; arbitrary 'improvements' often dilute original meaning and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make series readable from intended vantage points and sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical note on capitals: octagonal capitals have sides counted from the sea/Piazzetta; some capitals now have only three visible sides due to later walling up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange personified figures and scenes so their intended sequence and orientation are readable from the viewer's standpoint; consider which sides will be visible and design accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contraries as interpretive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin: 'In reading Dante, this mode of reasoning from contraries is a great help, for his philosophy of the vices is the only one which admits of classification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret and design moral systems by reasoning through oppositions—this clarifies classification and helps viewers/readers grasp the moral architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign penalties or consequences in proportion to moral weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin highlights Dante's intensity in punishing treason and in attaching severe penalties to sorrow (accidioso) to mark the duty of rejoicing in God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing moral order (e.g., in allegory or narrative), scale consequences and symbolic punishments proportionally to the perceived severity or social significance of the sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability: avoid unintelligible personifications without clarifying markers
rubrics_metrics.description: An example: 'It has no inscriptions, and its subjects are not, by themselves, intelligible; but they appear to be typical of the degradation of human instincts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If personifications are obscure, provide context (inscriptions, accompanying scenes, or explanatory placement) to prevent misreading; ambiguity may be artistic but risks losing the didactic point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider moral tone when selecting physical posture and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Many figures described by posture and expression (Patience with right hand on breast, left extended; Despair thrusting dagger into throat and tearing hair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pose figures and set facial expressions so they embody the moral quality intended—meekness, rage, despair, steadfastness—thus making the allegory psychologically credible.
